extracted.intended_audience: homeowners, builders, architects, and public-health practitioners concerned with sanitary house and stable construction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for siting and constructing houses and barns to promote healthfulness by controlling soil, water, ventilation, and related factors; includes specific recommendations for drains, walls, floors, cellars, privies, and stables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of soil and topography for health
rubrics_metrics.description: Soil and topography indirectly affect household health because rock types form different surface formations, some healthy and some unhealthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer sites where surface slope carries off drainage rapidly (e.g., granite near surface giving rapid slopes). Avoid sites prone to marshes or water-soaked valleys. Topography similar to regions with high cancer mortality (e.g., clay subsoil with thin surface soil and water-soaked valleys) should be treated with caution until causes are understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soil-type suitability (granite, limestone, sandstone, gravel, sand, clay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different soils have differing health implications: granite near the surface is usually healthy; limestone often has marshes and suspect drinking water; sandstone and sands/gravels are generally healthy; clays and heavy alluvial soils are undesirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gravel is best provided ground water reaches 3–4 feet below cellar bottom. Sand is fine unless mixed with decaying vegetable matter (which may yield nitrates in springs). Clay holds moisture and predisposes to dampness and marshes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of made ground (refuse-filled sites)
rubrics_metrics.description: Soils composed of garbage, street sweepings, or factory refuse are distinctly objectionable for building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if short-term mortality records don't show excess sickness, repeated breathing of air from such polluted soil is likely unhealthy. Organic matter buried in such soils decomposes slowly (years to decades) depending on conditions, so avoid building on refuse-filled land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of cultivation and manuring on health
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive cultivation and manured fields are not inherently unhealthy according to contemporary bacteriology; earlier fears (e.g., fever from plowed manured fields) lack evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do consider insect breeding as a secondary effect; the two essentials for health are topography (surface drainage) and character of soil (keeping ground water sufficiently deep).

rubrics_metrics.name: Soil air and gas ingress risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Air in soil voids is mobile and can be drawn into cellars and houses by suction from heated interiors or rising ground water, potentially carrying odors or pollutants (even from distant gas leaks or broken drains).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent ingress by providing an air- or water-tight layer between house and soil, and by draining away water that could force soil air into cellars. Waterproof outside cellar walls and provide an air-tight cellar floor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moisture in soils is undesirable but not a direct disease cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Damp soil has historically been thought to cause fevers and consumption, but modern understanding (e.g., discovery of malarial parasite) weakens that link; dampness is still undesirable for other reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid living over wet cellars because dampness fosters mold, damages the house, and can reduce household vitality, making disease more likely as a predisposing factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface grading to prevent water accumulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Slope ground surface away from house walls on all sides to prevent water accumulating against cellar walls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, slope at least ten feet away from house so there is no standing water. A fall of 1 foot in 100 is ample on grassy areas; slopes up to 7–8 feet per 100 are permissible but may be aesthetically objectionable. Provide proper outlets for collected water via pipes or surface depressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision and design of surface drains/gutters
rubrics_metrics.description: Where simple grading is insufficient, construct shallow trenches, paved ditches, or cement gutters to intercept surface water and carry it to a proper outlet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for snow accumulation and spring runoff when sizing and routing drains; ensure outlets lead into a stream, gulley, underground pipe, or depression with a free outlet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain and control ground water levels with subsoil drains
rubrics_metrics.description: Ground water levels fluctuate seasonally and may rise enough to flood cellars; a subsoil trench or drain system is necessary to limit the height of rising ground water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lay a system of drainpipes around the house extending to include the yard and to a free outlet; without a free outlet drains cannot be effective. Location on perfectly level bottom land is objectionable due to lack of natural outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of burnt-clay (tile) drains and spacing/grades
rubrics_metrics.description: Tile drains (burnt clay) are the proper material for underdrains; common tile is octagonal outside and circular inside, 1 foot long, 2–6 inch internal diameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laterals commonly 4-inch inside diameter; mains 6-inch (increase for long runs). Lay laterals about 15 feet apart (can be 20 ft in porous soil or up to 50 ft if tiles are >4 ft deep). Grade of tile: 1/4 inch per foot is proper; use engineer's level for accuracy. Entrances into a cross main (6 in. usually) that has a free outlet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of a competent survey for outlet determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding a practicable outlet for drains on level ground is difficult and should not be left to the untrained eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have an engineer with a level determine where a proper point of discharge may be found rather than risking long trenching with no outlet; small expenditure for survey saves much digging expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shutting out soil air: waterproofing and drains around cellar
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent soil air and moisture entering the cellar, interpose an air- or water-tight layer between house and soil and provide drains to remove accumulated water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Builders often neglect this; install thorough waterproof coating on outside walls and draintile laid properly with porous filling and at appropriate depth. Provide an air-tight floor over the cellar bottom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exterior wall-drains: specifications and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: A tile drain not less than 4 inches in diameter should be laid completely around the house to prevent moisture entering the cellar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grade not less than 6 inches in 100 feet. Highest point of drain should be 1 foot below bottom of concrete cellar floor (deeper at lower ends). Lay before foundations or in trenches after construction; fill around tile with coarse gravel to prevent siltation. In low available grade, two lines directly under cellar floor may be used (see interior drain layout).

rubrics_metrics.name: Position and design of outfall for drains
rubrics_metrics.description: The drain's discharge point must avoid freezing and ensure free delivery year-round, and be placed at a safe distance from the house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best to discharge to a brook where velocity prevents freezing or below water level; otherwise into a small covered cesspool if soil can absorb it and ground water allows. Ensure outfall is distant so overflow won't seep back to cellar walls; in cities, connection to public sewer allowed only if sewer is deep enough and ordinances permit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid loose (dry) stone cellar walls; prefer smooth-backed masonry
rubrics_metrics.description: Loose stone walls without mortar are not water-tight, allow rodents, and yield to earth pressure; rough-backed walls encourage water penetration and frost damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use smooth exterior backing so water runs off easily, fill joints with mortar, provide a proper surface for tar/asphalt coating. Avoid the rough-backed, projecting stones shown in poor practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide air-space in cellar walls to prevent dampness
rubrics_metrics.description: An air-space in cellar walls is the only way to ensure a dry cellar if the bottom is below ground-water level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options: use a 4-inch course of hollow brick on the inside; divide wall into two walls with ~3–4 inch space held by ties or special blocks. Figures illustrate wire ties, header lap, or terra-cotta blocks to hold the two parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of tar/asphalt and tar-paper for waterproofing walls
rubrics_metrics.description: Thorough plastering of exterior walls coated with hot tar or asphalted paint, and embedding layers of tar paper in tar, forms an effective waterproof barrier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paving asphalt with much bitumen slides; prefer asphalt oil or liquid asphalt. One method: build wall in two parts separated ~1/2 inch and fill with liquid asphalt; another: paint outside with hot tar and press in multiple layers of tar paper, overlapping and coated to make a continuous barrier enclosed between masonry so it cannot be injured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damp courses (horizontal waterproof layers) in walls
rubrics_metrics.description: Damp courses at about the level of the top of cellar floor (and sometimes at ground level) prevent moisture in cellar walls from rising into the above-ground masonry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple damp course: bring masonry level and paint top surface with liquid coal tar. Alternatively, paint masonry with liquid asphalt and embed asphalt-covered building paper, painted again to make a continuous horizontal waterproof layer. French methods and Price's sections are illustrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cellar floor composition and waterproofing
rubrics_metrics.description: Cellar floors should be covered with concrete and treated to prevent water or moisture rising through the floor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete mix: one part cement, three parts sand, six parts broken stone, or one part cement to eight parts gravel. Check gravel:sand proportion by sieving gravel and measuring displacement with water. Concrete is not water-tight—treat with denser cement-sand topping (3/4 inch of equal parts) or carry asphalt coating across floor (paint, paper, paint) then protect with brick laid flat or a 2-inch concrete layer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cellar ventilation and prevention of mosquito breeding
rubrics_metrics.description: Cellars must be ventilated to avoid musty, oxygen-deficient conditions; poor cellar air contributes to poor household health and allows mosquitoes to overwinter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open cellar windows (cover with coarse netting for animals and fine netting for insects). Avoid cisterns in cellars unless covered with mosquito netting. Ventilate storage areas; ensure cellar door/windows are used to admit fresh air and sunlight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privy (outside closet) placement and design for health
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary outside privy often exposes users to cold and contributes to digestive and respiratory disease risk; improvements can reduce health hazards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate privy closer to house (e.g., woodshed, barn corner, or moved up to back door with roofed passage) to avoid exposure. Use liberal earth in vaults to eliminate odors; employ water-tight boxes/buckets for frequent night-soil removal. Provide a small stove to warm the closet in cold weather to prevent users postponing evacuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable design: light, ventilation, and space per cow
rubrics_metrics.description: Barn/stable construction affects stock health; light and ventilation are primary for healthy stables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stable windows should be like house windows (two sashes, adjustable). In winter large sash may be closed with separate window for ventilation. For good health provide about 500 cubic feet of space per cow with active ventilation; avoid underground dugout stables with inadequate light.
